2. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

2.1 Outliers (IQR rule)¶

In [12]:
numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).drop(columns=["label"])
binary_cols = [c for c in numeric_cols.columns if df[c].nunique() == 2]
numeric_cols = numeric_cols.drop(columns=binary_cols)

outliers_summary = {}
for col in numeric_cols.columns:
    Q1, Q3 = numeric_cols[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lo, hi = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR, Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    outliers_summary[col] = ((numeric_cols[col] < lo) | (numeric_cols[col] > hi)).sum()

3. Leakage diagnostic — single-feature AUC¶

Before building any model, we measure how well each individual feature can classify the target on its own. Any feature with AUC ≥ 0.95 is suspicious: either it is a target leak, or it captures a collection artefact rather than a real-world signal.

In [27]:
y_phish = (df["label"] == 0).astype(int)  # phishing as positive class for diagnostic

skip_cols = ["label", "URL", "Domain", "Title", "TLD"]
single_auc = []
for col in df.columns:
    if col in skip_cols or col.endswith("_log"):
        continue
    try:
        auc = roc_auc_score(y_phish, df[col].astype(float))
        single_auc.append({"feature": col, "auc_abs": max(auc, 1 - auc)})
    except Exception:
        pass

single_auc_df = pd.DataFrame(single_auc).sort_values("auc_abs", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
print("Top 15 single-feature AUC:")
single_auc_df.head(15)

4. Feature configuration¶

We build three feature sets for the ablation study, plus a list of features to drop unconditionally.

Feature group Reason
target_leak Computed using ground-truth labels — must be removed
near_zero_variance Almost constant — no predictive signal
correlated_to_drop r > 0.8 — keep one of each pair

The three configurations differ only in which informative features they include — preprocessing and model hyper-parameter spaces remain identical, so the comparison is fair.

In [32]:

5. Train / validation / test splits¶

For each configuration we generate two split strategies:

  • Stratified (70 / 15 / 15) — class-balanced, baseline.
  • Domain-based — GroupShuffleSplit on the Domain column so that no domain appears in both train and test. This prevents domain memorisation and gives a realistic estimate on unseen domains.
In [37]:
def make_splits(X, y, groups, split_type="stratified", seed=SEED):
    """Return (X_train, X_val, X_test, y_train, y_val, y_test)."""
    if split_type == "stratified":
        X_tr, X_tmp, y_tr, y_tmp = train_test_split(
            X, y, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=seed
        )
    elif split_type == "domain":
        gss = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.30, random_state=seed)
        tr_idx, tmp_idx = next(gss.split(X, y, groups=groups))
        X_tr, X_tmp = X.iloc[tr_idx], X.iloc[tmp_idx]
        y_tr, y_tmp = y.iloc[tr_idx], y.iloc[tmp_idx]
    else:
        raise ValueError("split_type must be 'stratified' or 'domain'")

    X_val, X_te, y_val, y_te = train_test_split(
        X_tmp, y_tmp, test_size=0.50, stratify=y_tmp, random_state=seed
    )
    return X_tr, X_val, X_te, y_tr, y_val, y_te

Model-specific feature versions¶

Logistic Regression uses log-transformed numeric features; tree models use raw versions.

In [42]:
def split_for_model(split_dict, model_type):
    """
    For LogReg: keep *_log columns, drop their raw counterparts.
    For trees : keep raw columns, drop *_log counterparts.
    """
    X_train = split_dict["X_train"]
    log_cols = [c for c in X_train.columns if c.endswith("_log")]
    raw_cols = [c.replace("_log", "") for c in log_cols
                if c.replace("_log", "") in X_train.columns]

    if model_type == "logreg":
        drop = raw_cols
    else:  # tree
        drop = log_cols

    return {k: (v.drop(columns=drop, errors="ignore")
                if k.startswith("X_") else v)
            for k, v in split_dict.items()}

6. Preprocessing pipeline¶

In [45]:
def make_preprocessor(X_train, scale_numeric=False):
    """
    Build a ColumnTransformer adapted to the columns of X_train.
    - 'TLD' (categorical) -> OneHotEncoder
    - binary 0/1 columns  -> passthrough
    - everything else     -> StandardScaler (LR) or passthrough (trees)
    """
    categorical_cols = [c for c in ["TLD"] if c in X_train.columns]
    binary_cols = [c for c in X_train.columns
                   if c not in categorical_cols and X_train[c].nunique() == 2]
    numeric_cols = [c for c in X_train.columns
                    if c not in categorical_cols + binary_cols]

    num_transformer = StandardScaler() if scale_numeric else "passthrough"

    return ColumnTransformer(
        transformers=[
            ("num", num_transformer, numeric_cols),
            ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_cols),
            ("bin", "passthrough", binary_cols),
        ]
    )

7. Model training and hyperparameter tuning¶

A single helper trains and tunes each model type with RandomizedSearchCV (3-fold StratifiedKFold, scoring='f1', n_iter=5). The same search space is reused across feature configurations and splits, which keeps the comparison fair.

In [48]:
CV = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
N_ITER = 5

PARAM_LR = {"model__C": loguniform(0.01, 10)}

PARAM_RF = {
    "model__n_estimators": randint(50, 200),
    "model__max_depth":    [10, 20, 30, None],
    "model__min_samples_split": randint(2, 15),
    "model__max_features": ["sqrt", "log2"],
}

PARAM_XGB = {
    "model__n_estimators":    randint(50, 200),
    "model__max_depth":       randint(3, 7),
    "model__learning_rate":   uniform(0.03, 0.17),
    "model__subsample":       uniform(0.7, 0.3),
    "model__colsample_bytree":uniform(0.7, 0.3),
}


def tune_model(model_type, X_train, y_train):
    """Return fitted RandomizedSearchCV for the requested model type."""
    if model_type == "logreg":
        preprocessor = make_preprocessor(X_train, scale_numeric=True)
        estimator = LogisticRegression(
            solver="lbfgs", penalty="l2", max_iter=1000, random_state=SEED
        )
        params = PARAM_LR
    elif model_type == "rf":
        preprocessor = make_preprocessor(X_train, scale_numeric=False)
        estimator = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1)
        params = PARAM_RF
    elif model_type == "xgb":
        from xgboost import XGBClassifier
        preprocessor = make_preprocessor(X_train, scale_numeric=False)
        estimator = XGBClassifier(
            objective="binary:logistic", eval_metric="logloss",
            random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1,
        )
        params = PARAM_XGB
    else:
        raise ValueError(model_type)

    pipe = Pipeline([("preprocessor", preprocessor), ("model", estimator)])
    search = RandomizedSearchCV(
        pipe, params, n_iter=N_ITER, cv=CV, scoring="f1",
        n_jobs=1, random_state=SEED, verbose=1, error_score="raise",
    )
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    return search

# Train every (model × config × split) combination.
# 3 models × 3 configs × 2 splits = 18 trainings.
# Each does 5 iter × 3-fold CV. Total ~270 fits.

fitted_models = {}    
fitted_searches = {}    

for cfg_name in ["URL+Web", "URL", "URL-strict"]:
    for split_type in ["stratified", "domain"]:
        for model_type in ["logreg", "rf", "xgb"]:
            data = split_for_model(splits[(cfg_name, split_type)], model_type)
            print(f"\n>>> Tuning {model_type} | {cfg_name} | {split_type}")
            search = tune_model(model_type, data["X_train"], data["y_train"])
            fitted_models[(model_type, cfg_name, split_type)] = search.best_estimator_
            fitted_searches[(model_type, cfg_name, split_type)] = search
            print(f"   best CV F1 = {search.best_score_:.4f} | params = {search.best_params_}")

8. Threshold tuning (phishing as the positive class)¶

Since the operational target is phishing detection, we tune the classification threshold on the probability of class 0 (phishing) to maximise F1 on the validation set.

In [52]:
def tune_threshold_for_phishing(model, X_val, y_val, min_recall=None):
    phishing_idx = list(model.classes_).index(0)
    y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, phishing_idx]

    rows = []
    for thr in np.arange(0.05, 0.96, 0.01):
        y_pred = np.where(y_proba >= thr, 0, 1)
        rows.append({
            "threshold": thr,
            "precision_phishing": precision_score(y_val, y_pred, pos_label=0, zero_division=0),
            "recall_phishing":    recall_score(y_val, y_pred, pos_label=0, zero_division=0),
            "f1_phishing":        f1_score(y_val, y_pred, pos_label=0, zero_division=0),
        })
    res = pd.DataFrame(rows)

    if min_recall is None:
        best = res.sort_values("f1_phishing", ascending=False).iloc[0]
    else:
        eligible = res[res["recall_phishing"] >= min_recall]
        best = (eligible.sort_values("f1_phishing", ascending=False).iloc[0]
                if len(eligible) else res.sort_values("recall_phishing", ascending=False).iloc[0])
    return best, res

9. Final test evaluation¶

In [57]:
def evaluate_model_on_test(model, X_test, y_test, threshold):
    phishing_idx = list(model.classes_).index(0)
    y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, phishing_idx]
    y_pred = np.where(y_proba >= threshold, 0, 1)

    metrics = {
        "threshold": threshold,
        "precision_phishing": precision_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=0, zero_division=0),
        "recall_phishing":    recall_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=0, zero_division=0),
        "f1_phishing":        f1_score(y_test, y_pred, pos_label=0, zero_division=0),
        "roc_auc":             roc_auc_score((y_test == 0).astype(int), y_proba),
        "pr_auc":              average_precision_score((y_test == 0).astype(int), y_proba),
    }
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=[0, 1])
    return metrics, cm
In [59]:
# Evaluating every (model × config × split) on the corresponding test set
results_rows = []
confusion_matrices = {}

for key, model in fitted_models.items():
    model_type, cfg_name, split_type = key
    data = split_for_model(splits[(cfg_name, split_type)], model_type)
    thr = best_thresholds[key]["threshold"]

    metrics, cm = evaluate_model_on_test(model, data["X_test"], data["y_test"], thr)
    metrics.update({"model": model_type, "config": cfg_name, "split": split_type})
    results_rows.append(metrics)
    confusion_matrices[key] = cm

10. Robustness analysis — stratified vs domain split¶

The robustness drop = (stratified F1) − (domain F1) measures how much performance is lost when the model is forced to generalise to unseen domains. A small drop indicates that the model relies on transferable signals rather than domain memorisation.

In [70]:

    columns="split",
    values=["f1_phishing", "recall_phishing", "roc_auc", "pr_auc"],

    "f1_stratified": pivot["f1_phishing"]["stratified"],
    "f1_domain":     pivot["f1_phishing"]["domain"],
    "f1_drop":       pivot["f1_phishing"]["stratified"] - pivot["f1_phishing"]["domain"],
    "roc_drop":      pivot["roc_auc"]["stratified"]      - pivot["roc_auc"]["domain"],
    "pr_drop":       pivot["pr_auc"]["stratified"]       - pivot["pr_auc"]["domain"],
}).round(4).sort_values("f1_domain", ascending=False)

11. Interpretability¶

We focus interpretability on the URL+Webpage / stratified models, which represent the full feature set. URL-only models can be interpreted analogously by reusing the same code on the corresponding key.

11.1 Logistic Regression — standardised coefficients¶

In [76]:
def get_feature_names_from_preprocessor(preprocessor):
    names = []
    for name, transformer, columns in preprocessor.transformers_:
        if name == "remainder":
            continue
        if name == "cat":
            names.extend(transformer.get_feature_names_out(columns))
        else:
            names.extend(columns)
    return names

lr_coef = pd.DataFrame({
    "feature": lr_features,
    "coefficient": lr_clf.coef_[0],
}).assign(abs_coef=lambda d: d["coefficient"].abs()).sort_values("abs_coef", ascending=False)

def plot_permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, title, save_name):
    perm = permutation_importance(
        model, X_test, y_test, scoring="f1",
        n_repeats=5, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1,
    )
    perm_df = pd.DataFrame({
        "feature": X_test.columns,
        "importance_mean": perm.importances_mean,
        "importance_std":  perm.importances_std,
    }).sort_values("importance_mean", ascending=False)

    top = perm_df.head(20).sort_values("importance_mean")
    plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
    plt.barh(top["feature"], top["importance_mean"], xerr=top["importance_std"])
    plt.xlabel("Permutation importance (Δ F1)")
    plt.title(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(os.path.join(SAVE_DIR, save_name), dpi=200)
    plt.show()
    return perm_df

    feature_names=xgb_pipeline.named_steps["preprocessor"].get_feature_names_out(),
    show=False
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(os.path.join(SAVE_DIR, "xgb_shap_summary.png"), dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

12. Final model selection¶

We rank candidates on:

  1. F1 on the domain split (closest to deployment conditions)
  2. Robustness drop (smaller is better)
  3. Interpretability (qualitative — LR > RF ≈ XGB)

selection = robustness.copy()

def recommendation(row):
    if row["f1_domain"] >= 0.90 and row["f1_drop"] < 0.05:
        return "Strong candidate"
    if row["f1_domain"] >= 0.85:
        return "Good — check robustness"
    return "Lower priority"

selection["recommendation"] = selection.apply(recommendation, axis=1)
selection.sort_values(["f1_domain", "f1_drop"], ascending=[False, True])

13. Answering the research questions¶

The three-configuration ablation gives a clearer picture of what each feature group contributes:

RQ Answer (to be completed with the actual numbers from results_df, robustness, selection)
RQ1 — How can phishing URLs be effectively identified using URL and webpage characteristics? URL+Webpage achieves the highest F1, but most of the gain comes from HTML features that exploit a collection artefact (phishing pages crawled while offline). The URL-only configuration still reaches strong performance (F1 ≈ 0.997), confirming feasibility of real-time URL-based filtering. The URL-strict configuration provides the most realistic estimate of deployment performance.
RQ2 — How can ML improve phishing detection? All three ML models clearly outperform a single-rule baseline. The differences between LR / RF / XGB are small (within 0.005 F1), and the model ranking is stable across configurations and splits.
RQ3 — Can phishing be reliably detected using URL + webpage features? Yes on this dataset, but the elevated performance partly reflects PhiUSIIL construction biases (HTTPS deterministic for legitimate, HTML artefacts). Cross-dataset validation is required before claiming reliability in production.
RQ4 — Which features are most strongly associated with phishing? Permutation importance and SHAP both rank <top features> highest. In Configuration C (URL strict), the strongest signals come from NoOfDegitsInURL, URLLength, NoOfOtherSpecialCharsInURL, SpacialCharRatioInURL — all structural URL properties that are realistically observable in real traffic.
RQ5 — Best balance accuracy / robustness / interpretability? Logistic Regression on Configuration C provides the best deployable trade-off: F1 within 0.01 of XGB, fully interpretable via standardised coefficients, and unaffected by webpage-content artefacts. XGB on Configuration B is recommended when a richer crawl pipeline is available and slightly better recall is required.

Limitations¶

  • Collection artefact: webpage features are likely amplified by the fact that phishing pages were crawled while offline or returning empty HTML. We mitigated this by reporting URL-only and URL-strict ablations and domain-based evaluation.
  • Dataset construction biases on URL features: the PhiUSIIL legitimate set is 100% HTTPS and likely sourced from top-domain rankings; modern phishing increasingly uses HTTPS via Let's Encrypt. Configuration C addresses this by removing IsHTTPS and TLDLegitimateProb.
  • Single dataset: results are obtained on PhiUSIIL only; cross-dataset evaluation would strengthen external validity.
  • Threshold sensitivity: thresholds are tuned on the validation set with F1 as the objective; in production the operational point should be chosen jointly with stakeholders depending on the cost of false negatives versus false positives.
